newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Rising Chinese power spark jitters among neighbours.
newsitem.headline: Rising Chinese power spark jitters among neighbours.

text.p: The rising tide of Chinese military power and its drive for regional naval supremacy has its neighbours worried, officials and analysts say.
"Will China decide to pursue hegemony and carve out a sphere of influence of its own?" Philippine President Fidel Ramos asked in a speech in Los Angeles last week.

He said China's behaviour over the disputed Spratly Islands in the South China Sea was "for us, the litmus test of whether China -- as a great power -- intends to play by international rules or makes its own."

Worasak Mattanobol, a specialist in Chinese military affairs at Chulalongkorn University in Thailand, summed up some of the fears in the region, saying: "China is building up its naval strength because it wants to show the world it is big brother in this region."
China has recently acquired two Russian guided missile cruisers and plans to add an aircraft carrier to its fleet by the turn of the century.
That has added to the regional concerns, driven in Southeast Asia by the Spratlys dispute and by spats between Beijing, Tokyo and Taiwan over the Diaoyu or Senkaku islands.

The Philippines recently protested against the presence of three Chinese warships near parts of the Spratlys that Manila claims. Beijing and Tokyo were again embroiled in a dispute when a Japanese legislator landed on the Diaoyus/Senkakus last week.
Worry about China is also fuelled by doubts over whether the United States has the long-term will to maintain its defence umbrella over the region.
The commander of U.S. naval forces in Japan, Rear Admiral Michael Haskins, said last week there would be no reduction in the 100,000 U.S. soldiers in the region.

"This regional presence underwrites political and economic stability," he told a naval conference in Singapore. The U.S. role would continue to be to "deter the rise of any hegemonistic power or coalition."

John Downing, naval defence analyst at the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies, said China "believes that she must achieve regional military supremacy in order to assert authority over neighbouring states."
But China's ability to project power over areas like the Diaoyus or the Spratlys remains limited, and its amphibious forces are vulnerable to air attack, analysts say.

"The Chinese navy is developing rapidly, (but) I don't think any coalition of Western navies, or even the U.S. navy on its own...need fear the (Chinese) navy greatly," said a Western defence attache in Beijing.

Downing said China's navy has 1,100 ships, more than the United States. But most are devoted to coastal defence. It has one submarine armed with nuclear-tipped ballistic missiles and 54 destroyers and frigates, most of them more than 25 years old.

"Command and control, electronics and anti-submarine warfare systems are all assessed as poor by modern standards. The bulk of the navy...have only a very limited air defence capability," he told the Singapore conference.
Still, China's economic boom means more money for the navy.

"Given their tremendous growth rate, I think in a decade the Chinese will be able to project themselves sufficiently both in naval and air terms," said Blas Ople, the chairman of the Philippine Senate Foreign relations committee.

"Given its efforts in building up its navy in the past decade, China will undoubtedly become a naval power over the next few years and no other Asian country would be able to counter it," a military expert in Taiwan said.

Juwono Sudarsono, of the Indonesia's National Resilience Institute government think tank, agreed China would become a major power in the next 10 years but must be careful about wrecking its relations with the region.
"China has to weigh the repercussions of any such behaviour against the goodwill they still need to promote trade and investment," Juwono said.
Ople, however, believess China's growth will give it "a potential for mischief".
"If China makes a move to annex the whole of the South China Sea and impede freedom of navigation there, then there will be trouble, especially from Japan," he said.
